prs.title: Turbopack: don't scope hoist modules using direct eval
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Turbopack scope hoisting no longer merges modules that contain a direct `eval(...)` call. Such modules are emitted as their own module factories, and the rest of the graph is still merged.

### Why?

Merging puts modules into one shared scope and renames colliding top-level bindings. A direct `eval` resolves names at runtime against its lexical scope, so after a rename it can read the wrong binding. For example, `eval('local')` can return another module's `local`, or throw.

### How?

- **Detection:** while building the analyzer's variable graph, each call expression is checked. If the callee (with parentheses stripped) is the unresolved global `eval` identifier, a module-wide flag is set. Nested functions, classes and IIFEs are covered.
- **What doesn't count:** indirect forms leave the module mergeable. These are `(0, eval)(…)`, `globalThis.eval(…)`, `eval?.(…)`, aliases, `new eval(…)`, and a locally bound `eval`.
- **Plumbing:** the flag is passed into the module analysis result, and `EcmascriptModuleAsset::is_mergeable` returns `false` when it is set. The existing rule that only ESM modules are mergeable is unchanged.
- **Split modules:** a module with exports can be split into a facade plus a `<locals>` module. The `<locals>` module carries the original code but used the trait's default `is_mergeable`, which is always `true`, so it would have bypassed the opt-out. It now uses the original module's answer.

### Tests

- **Analyzer unit test:** covers direct, in
…(truncated)

prs.title: turbopack: intern merge bitmaps in compute_merged_modules
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Interns the merge bitmaps in `compute_merged_modules` (turbopack-core, `module_graph/merged_modules.rs`). Each distinct `RoaringBitmapWrapper` gets a dense `u32` id once, after the fixed-point traversal. The `map chunk groups` and `exposed computation` traversals then key `chunk_lists` by that id and compare ids instead of bitmaps.

This is the first of three stacked PRs that speed up `compute_merged_modules`:
1. intern bitmaps (this PR)
2. parallel merge of the chunk group lists (#100237)
3. reconciliation shortcuts (#100238)

### Why?

`map chunk groups` visits every module of every chunk group (about 19.8 M visits on the bench app below). On each visit, the old code:
- looked up `chunk_lists: FxHashMap<&RoaringBitmapWrapper, _>`, where `RoaringBitmapWrapper::hash` serializes the whole bitmap into the hasher;
- compared the parent's and the child's bitmaps.

In a CPU profile, `serialize_into` under that hash accounted for about two thirds of the phase's samples.

### How?

- **`intern_bitmaps`:** a small private helper that maps each key to the id of its bitmap. Equal bitmaps (by `RoaringBitmapWrapper`'s `Eq`) get the same id.
- **Equivalence:** id equality is exactly bitmap equality, so the lists, their order and the output are unchanged.
- **Tracing:** an `intern bitmaps` span shows the cost of interning (~35 ms on the bench app).

### Results

Bench app `bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages` at 32 CPUs:
- **Builds:** cold `next build` with `taskset 0-31` an

prs.title: turbo-persistence: read SST metadata blocks once with pread
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

Reads each SST's block-offset table and index block once at open, with positional reads, store the data in a heap buffer, instead of dereferencing the mmap

The offset table becomes a validated `BlockOffsets` value. Lookup handles keep the index block as an owned array of entries. Both are owned outside the backing enums.

### Why?

Every block access needs two offset-table entries, and every lookup binary searches the index block. Reading both with `pread` and keeping them in memory means locating a block never reads either of them through the mmap.

Currently the offset block is advised as `WILLNEED` on open, but this is not sufficient, it will ensure it is quickly availble after startup, but the memory remains `madvise(RANDOM)` so it does not participate in recency accounting.  However, these are the hottest blocks in any SST since all accesses reference them.

Alternatively we could `madvise(DEFAULT)` this range, but the `pread` is more accurate (our data is not page aligned anyway, but the pread is perfectly accurate

The difference will probably only matter if mmap table pages are being reclaimed.

prs.title: Use os.availableParallelism() instead of os.cpus().length
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Use [`os.availableParallelism()`](https://nodejs.org/api/os.html#osavailableparallelism) instead of `os.cpus().length` wherever we need a CPU count:

- default `experimental.cpus` (build worker count)
- `next info` CPU cores output
- dev server trace span and trace upload `cpus` metadata
- anonymous telemetry `cpuCount`
- devlow-bench `NUM_CPUS`

### Why?

`os.cpus().length` reports every logical CPU on the host and can be `0` on some platforms. `os.availableParallelism()` estimates the parallelism actually available to the process, respecting CPU affinity, and always returns at least 1. That avoids spawning more workers than the process can effectively use on constrained machines and in containers.

### How?

- The worker default keeps its existing policy (`CIRCLE_NODE_TOTAL` override, subtract one, minimum of one). The `os.cpus() || { length: 1 }` fallback is no longer needed, because the API always returns at least 1 and our Node.js minimum (20.9) supports it.
- Reporting and telemetry fields keep their names and types. On constrained machines their values may now be lower, reflecting the usable parallelism.
- `os.cpus()` stays where we need CPU model or speed information rather than a count.

prs.title: Clarify lazy SST opening in turbo-persistence docs
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## What?

Fixes how the turbo-persistence README describes opening the database and reading from it. The old text said every SST file is memory mapped up front.

## Why?

The old wording overstated how much memory opening a database costs. In the current implementation:

- Opening the database loads only the meta files (memory mapped, or read into heap memory in `AccessMode::File`). It parses their AMQFs and filters out obsolete entries. SST and blob files are not opened.
- An SST file is opened lazily, the first time a lookup gets past its hash-range and AMQF checks, and is then cached on its meta entry.
- `AccessMode::File` never memory maps SST files. It keeps the block offset table on the heap and reads blocks with positioned reads.
- In either mode, opening an SST reads and verifies only its index block. Key and value blocks are read when a lookup needs them.

## How?

- Updates the **Opening** steps to match the directory-loading code.
- Adds a short lifecycle explanation to **Reading**, covering both access modes and what drives memory cost.
- Corrects the lookup outline:
  - adds the hash-range check
  - says the AMQF lives in the meta file
  - shows where the SST is opened

Documentation only. The wording was checked against `Db::load_directory`, `MetaEntry::sst`, `MetaFile::lookup_entry` and `StaticSortedFile::open`.

prs.title: remove Static render stage
prs.author: lubieowoce
prs.body:
Since the introduction of `NavigationStatic`, the `Static` stage hasn't really been very useful, but we kept it as a "marker" stage that delineates where a static prerender ends (after `NavigationStatic`, containing all the finished accumulators).

However, things get weird in the presence of caches with hanging inputs, because `createHangingInputAbortSignal` waits until `finalStage` (currently `Static`), which means that the keys for caches with hanging inputs would only finish in the `Static` stage. We were still running the `Static` stage in a separate task, before resolving the accumulators, so in practice this didn't cause any problems, but semantically we expect all userspace code to be done after the `NavigationStatic` task, and this behavior of caches breaks that expectation.

I don't want to risk any weird staging bugs because of this, so removing `Static` seems like the easy choice.

prs.title: turbo-persistence: read compaction inputs with pread instead of mmap
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

Compaction iterated its input SST files through an mmap with `MADV_SEQUENTIAL`. This does not fit the block layout pattern (which tends to be ValueBlock, ValueBlock, KeyBlock....) because iteration starts from key blocks, so the readahead isn't well targeted.  OS level reclaim can recover this memory but it isn't eager and we _know_ after reading a block that we don't need it any more.

`StaticSortedFileIter`, which only compaction uses, now always reads blocks with `pread` into owned buffers, independent of the overall database's `AccessMode`, so an open input file holds only the blocks it currently uses.

This also enhances SharedBytes with a mechanism to be constructed from an `uninit` buffer (useful for decompression and `pread` targets).  This unifies a few codepaths and allows us to avoid some small buffer copies.

### Measurements

Full compaction on Linux (podman VM, kernel 7.2, XFS on virtio, page cache dropped before each run, single threaded), 2 rounds:

| | time | max RSS | peak mapped file pages |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 GB zstd database, values 16 B – 8 KiB, mmap (before) | 2.10 / 2.33 s | 315 MB | 301 – 318 MB |
| same, `pread` (this PR) | 2.07 / 2.04 s | 10 MB | 5 MB |
| 230 MB database of 16Mi tiny entries, mmap (before) | 2.73 / 2.64 s | 245 MB | 201 MB |
| same, `pread` (this PR) | 2.35 / 2.37 s | 57 MB | 6 MB |

The cgroup's `memory.peak` is the same in both, since it is dominated by page cache, which is charged either way and reclaimable: with

prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

Narrows the invalidations a warm `next dev` start triggers when project options are republished:

- `Project` keeps the draft-mode (preview) props in their own cell instead of inlining them.
- `EnvMap` uses keyed cells, and `EnvMap::read(name)` depends only on the requested variable.

Every dev start republishes the project options, and two of them always differ from the previous run: the preview props are randomly regenerated, and the env contains per-process values like `NEXT_PRIVATE_START_TIME`. prs.title: turbopack: store unused reference edges in a keyed Vc
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Moves the unused reference edges of `BindingUsageInfo` into their own keyed Turbo Tasks value, `UnusedReferenceEdges`. `ModuleGraphSnapshot` now holds only those edges, not the full binding usage info.

### Why?

`ModuleGraphSnapshot` needs binding usage info for one thing: deciding which graph edges to skip during traversal. Because the edge set was stored inline in `BindingUsageInfo`, graph snapshots depended on all of the binding usage info. Any change to the edges also changed `BindingUsageInfo` itself, which invalidated readers that only needed the other data (export usage, circuit breakers, partial-namespace modules).

### How?

- `BindingUsageInfo` stores the unused edges as a `ResolvedVc` to the new `cell = "keyed"` transparent set and exposes it via `unused_references_edges()`.
- `ModuleGraph` and `ModuleGraphLayer` read only that value into their snapshots. The removed `is_reference_unused_edge` helper is replaced by keyed `contains_key` checks on the edge set at the traversal sites.
- Traversals are synchronous, so the snapshot holds a `ReadRef` of the edge set. Traversal behavior is unchanged: the same edges are skipped and the double-analysis guard still fires.

### Verification

- `cargo check -p turbopack-core -p turbopack-cli`
- `cargo check -p next-core -p next-api`
- `cargo clippy -p turbopack-core -p turbopack-cli --all-targets`
- `cargo test -p turbopack-core --lib`

prs.title: Turbopack: propagate late partial namespace provenance to passthrough targets
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Namespace provenance from a late partial-namespace read now reaches the module's passthrough targets, even when that module was already processed with `All` usage or with the same names.

### Why?

`compute_binding_usage_info` tracks modules read through a namespace value (`namespace_object_may_escape`). Export-name mangling uses this to keep original names. Passthrough edges such as `export * from './y'` forward that provenance to their target.

Take a module that was reached first through a plain named or `All` edge, so its passthrough edge has already run. If a partial-namespace edge for it arrives later and adds no new export names, the module joins the provenance set but the visitor reports no change. It is never revisited, so its passthrough target stays out of the set.

### How?

Direct partial-namespace edges now count adding the target to the provenance set as a change, the same way the passthrough branch already does. The export-usage merge still always runs. Each module can only be added to the set once, so this triggers at most one extra revisit per module and the fixed point still terminates.

- the plain usage of `x` being `All` or an already-used name
- the namespace read arriving on the longer path (

prs.title: turbopack: use reverse postorder priority in compute_chunk_group_info
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## Summary

`compute_chunk_group_info` runs a fixed-point traversal over the module graph, ordered by BFS (minimum) depth. A module can gain new chunk groups after it was already visited, for example through a longer path from another entry or from a chunk group that is created later. When that happens, it is queued again and its whole subgraph is propagated again. On app-shaped graphs this means many visits per module.

This PR adds `ModuleGraphSnapshot::reverse_postorder_ranks`. It ranks every module by the reverse postorder of a DFS from the entries, using an iterative DFS that resolves `VisitedModule` aliases to the canonical node. Using `Reverse(rank)` as the priority visits a module only after all of its importers, except across cycles. On a DAG, each module is therefore visited exactly once.

`compute_chunk_group_info` now uses this rank instead of its own BFS depth pass.

`traverse_edges_fixed_point_with_priority` also now tracks initial entries in `queue_set`:
- an entry reachable from another entry is no longer queued twice;
- duplicate entries are ignored.

This is the first PR of a stack. `collect_graph` (#100429) and `compute_merged_modules` (#100430) follow in separate PRs.

### Benchmarks

**Setup:**
- `next build --experimental-build-mode compile` with Turbopack.
- `next-swc` release builds (LTO disabled and 16 codegen units, to keep the native builds feasible).
- Binaries interleaved per run, 3 runs each, `.next` removed before each run.
- Time is the BFS dep

prs.title: turbo-tasks: batch schedule invalidated tasks and cell dependents
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Tasks that become dirty together are handed to the turbo-tasks scheduler (`PriorityRunner`) as one batch instead of one by one, at two sites:

- `invalidate()` (explicit invalidation of a set of tasks)
- `invalidate_cell_dependents()` in `update_cell` (all dependents of a changed cell — the main fan-out path)

Also adds a `cell_fan_out` criterion benchmark to `turbo-tasks-backend`.

### Why?

`PriorityRunner` keeps all non-lowest-priority work in a `Mutex<BinaryHeap>`. Scheduling N tasks one by one locks that heap up to N times and grows it incrementally, contending with the workers that pop from it. This is a first step towards reducing that contention.

Note: in-tree, `invalidate()` is currently only reached with a single task (`TurboTasks::invalidate` → `Backend::invalidate_task`); `invalidate_tasks` / `invalidate_tasks_set` have no in-tree callers. The real fan-out is a cell change invalidating its dependents, which is why `update_cell` is batched too.

### How?

- **`PriorityRunner::schedule_many`**: behaves like calling `schedule` for each item. While there is free worker capacity, items are handed directly to new workers using the same slot reservation as `schedule`. The remaining items are queued in bulk: each item is still inserted into the claimable map before its key is published, lowest-priority keys still go to the lock-free queue, and all other keys are staged and then pushed into the heap under a single lock acquisition after one `reserve`. prs.title: Defer app router HMR refresh until the router is initialized
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

In dev, an app-router HMR refresh that arrives before the app router has initialized is no longer dropped. It now runs once the router mounts. Several early requests are coalesced into the newest one.

### Why?

`client/app-index.tsx` opens the HMR WebSocket before the initial RSC payload resolves and before `hydrateRoot`. `dispatch` is only set when `useActionQueue` renders. If an `ADDED_PAGE` / `REMOVED_PAGE` / `SERVER_COMPONENT_CHANGES` / `STATIC_PARAMS_CHANGED` message arrives in that window, `hmrRefresh()` throws `Internal Next.js error: Router action dispatched before initialization.` and the refresh is lost. The page then keeps showing stale content until a manual reload.

This shows up as the second failure mode of `test/e2e/app-dir/not-found/basic` › "should render the 404 page when the file is removed, and restore the page when re-added". The page is removed, the browser full-reloads to the 404, and the "page re-added" refresh arrives during hydration. The page stays on "Root Not Found" and the restore assertion times out.

### How?

The race is resolved in `use-action-queue.ts`, where `dispatch` is initialized:

- `dispatchAppRouterAction`: in dev, an `ACTION_HMR_REFRESH` that arrives while `dispatch` is still `null` is stored as the pending HMR refresh instead of throwing. A later early refresh replaces it. Its `AbortSignal` belongs to the newest generation, since `hmrRefresh` already aborts superseded ones.
